text:
Let  
\[
c=\frac{h}{4\pi},\qquad 
A_y=c\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The characteristic equation is
\[
\det(A_y-aI)
=\begin{vmatrix}-a&-ic\\ ic&-a\end{vmatrix}
=a^2-c^2=0.
\]
Hence
\[
a_\pm=\pm c=\pm\frac{h}{4\pi}.
\]

The corresponding normalized eigenvectors are
\[
\phi_+=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ i\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\phi_-=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-i\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Because \(A_y\) is Hermitian, its eigenvalues are real, eliminating (B) and (D). Also, for a spin-\(\tfrac12\) particle,
\[
A^2=A_x^2+A_y^2+A_z^2
=3c^2I,
\]
so every spinor, including \(\phi_\pm\), is an eigenfunction of \(A^2\). However,
\[
A_z\phi_+=c\phi_-,\qquad A_z\phi_-=c\phi_+,
\]
so these are not eigenfunctions of \(A_z\), consistent with \([A_y,A_z]\neq0\). The displayed matrix is written in the \(A_z\) basis, whose basis vectors are not the \(A_y\) eigenvectors.

Answer: C
